questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14065811/assets/1617a8efd9110fa435dc396d90450c7fe17d18105e2358ab5610135e32a385ad.png)

The half-ellipse above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +h,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +k\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(-3,-1),$ $a=4$ and $b=2.$  Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a half-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse and the line parallel to the $x$-axis and crossing the center of the ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14065811/assets/4659fda20ed9a2b5e5c10d60f504e4db378efb0bfe9ae037f4998511e75300cb.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\pi ]$, we get the half-ellipse.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the half-ellipse are 

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\theta \in [0,\pi ].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse
questions.problem:
The Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=9\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$

is given by

{{field-1}}
$=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{9} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{9}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{81} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{4\sqrt{3}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(4\sqrt{3})^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{48} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{81}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{48}={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{81}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{48}=1.
$$
